titre: The Terracotta Army’s Weapons Were Not Chrome-Plated
accroche: A 2019 study of 464 bronze weapons from the Terracotta Army put an end to the idea of an anti-rust treatment two thousand years old.
contenu_vulgarise:
On March 29, 1974, Yang Zhifa, his five brothers and their neighbor Wang Puzhi are digging a well in the Lintong district, near Xi’an, in Shaanxi province. Their shovels strike a clay head. Zhao Kangmin, curator of the local museum, is among the first to arrive: villagers have already carried fragments home, but he recognizes heads, torsos, limbs. He loads everything onto three trucks and sets about assembling it, some pieces no bigger than a fingernail. Fearing the hostility of factions still active at the end of the Cultural Revolution, he keeps the discovery secret. A journalist eventually lets it out, and Beijing orders a large-scale excavation.

## The mechanism

Among the eight thousand clay soldiers buried to accompany Emperor Qin Shi Huang, some bronze weapons, swords, spearheads, crossbow triggers, bear traces of chromium. For decades, one explanation is taken for granted in reference books and documentaries alike: Qin dynasty craftsmen supposedly applied a chromium coating to protect the metal, more than two thousand years before the West filed, in 1937, the patent for industrial chrome plating.

A team led by Marcos Martinón-Torres tests this explanation across the entire site. In 2019, it analyzes 464 bronze weapon pieces by portable X-ray fluorescence. Chromium, at a detection threshold of 0.1% by weight, appears on only 37 of them, or 8% of the sample, and very unevenly: 88% of sword and spear pommels, 75% of crossbow triggers, but no blades. This distribution fits no manufacturing pattern and no identifiable production batch.

Further analyses, electron microscopy and Raman spectroscopy, show that the chromium actually comes from the lacquer applied to the weapons and armor, itself rich in this element for a reason still poorly understood. The burial soil, for its part, contains less than a hundred parts per million of chromium. The study concludes: “The chromium anti-rust treatment theory should therefore be abandoned.”

## The shift

If chromium explains nothing, what preserved these bronzes for two thousand two hundred years? The same researchers point to a slightly alkaline soil, with a pH of 8.1 to 8.5, made of very fine particles, low in organic matter and poorly aerated, combined with tin-rich alloys that themselves form a protective layer. In an accelerated aging test, a control buried in this soil stays intact, while a control placed in a more acidic organic soil corrodes.

The lesson is not only about chemistry. For years, a partial correlation, a little chromium on some well-preserved pieces, was enough to hold up an appealing theory: a Chinese technological lead of two millennia over the West. It took measuring all 464 pieces, not just a handful, to see that this correlation did not survive at the scale of the entire site.

carte.punch: The chromium on the Terracotta Army’s weapons did not come from an anti-rust treatment.
carte.idee: For decades, it was believed that Qin craftsmen chrome-plated their weapons to protect them, two thousand years before the West. A 2019 study of 464 pieces shows that this chromium comes from nearby lacquer: it is the slightly alkaline soil that preserved the bronze.

quiz.question: Why does finding chromium on only 8% of the 464 weapons analyzed contradict the theory of a deliberate anti-rust treatment?
choix: Because a treatment by Qin craftsmen would affect all the pieces in a batch, not a minority unrelated to manufacturing
Because 8% is too high a rate to correspond to accidental contamination
Because bronze weapons physically could not retain chromium for more than a few years
Because the 0.1% detection threshold is too low to be reliable
quiz.explication: A deliberate anti-rust treatment, applied by the craftsmen, would be found on all the pieces of the same manufacturing batch. Here, chromium affects a minority of pieces (8%), distributed with no link to production batches, which matches accidental contamination and not an intended technical act.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the 2019 study, where does the chromium found on some of the Terracotta Army’s bronze weapons come from?
choix: From contamination by the chromium-rich lacquer applied to nearby weapons and armor
From a naturally chromium-rich bronze alloy used by Qin craftsmen
From a decorative pigment applied to the pommels for aesthetic reasons
From the burial soil, rich in chromium-bearing minerals
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The study attributes the chromium to post-depositional contamination by the nearby lacquer, itself rich in chromium for a reason not yet explained. The soil, by contrast, contains less than a hundred parts per million of chromium, which rules out the last two options; no chromium-bearing bronze alloy has been identified either.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the study, what really explains the good preservation of the Terracotta Army’s bronze weapons?
choix: A slightly alkaline, very fine-grained soil, combined with tin-rich bronzes
The chromium coating applied by Qin craftsmen
The total absence of moisture in the Shaanxi region for two thousand years
A protective varnish applied by archaeologists during the 1974 excavation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The study identifies a soil with a pH of 8.1 to 8.5, with very fine particles and low in organic matter, as well as the tin content of the bronzes, as preservation factors. Chromium is explicitly ruled out as a cause, and neither a modern varnish nor absolute dryness is involved.
